old: SIGNUP PATH, read today. The account is created at https://signup.oraclecloud.com/ and nowhere else; oracle.com/cloud/free is the marketing page and signup.cloud.oracle.com serves the same shell. The page is a React application whose HTML carries no form, so the field list is taken from Oracle's own signup document, which walks the same form step by step. In order: country (some countries, Russia named, need the Terms accepted by checkbox), name, email, CAPTCHA, an email verification link valid 30 minutes, a password of 8-40 characters with upper, lower, digit and symbol, an optional company, a cloud account name, a home region that cannot be changed afterwards, the Terms, then address and phone number, then the card, then 'Start my free trial'. There is no identity document and no company requirement; the company field is explicitly optional. The home region matters more than the card: a home region may not exist in the registrant's country, so an adjacent one must be picked, and the region cannot be changed, so a wrong pick is a new account. THE GRANT IS TWO PRODUCTS, not one. Always Free is the unlimited-period allowance described in free_tier.stated. The USD 300 is a separate 30-day trial that begins at the same signup and expires on its own; the FAQ says Always Free resources survive that expiry, but anything created with trial credit is reclaimed. So 'USD 300 for 90 days' is not what Oracle sells here: it is USD 300 for 30 days plus a permanent allowance. THE HOLD IS USD 1.00, published by Oracle's billing documentation, not by the signup page; the signup page says only 'a small, temporary charge' and names no amount. THE FAILURE MODE is the reason this row is a caveat and not a yes. Oracle refuses signups with a message that names three causes and no remedy, and two 2026 threads on Oracle's own forum show it arriving from Saudi Arabia and from a card that had just verified successfully. The country page says the tier is available wherever commercial OCI runs; there is no OCI region in Viet Nam, Thailand, Indonesia or the Philippines, so a registrant in one of those picks an adjacent region, and Oracle's fraud checks read the mismatch between the declared address and the connection. That is reported, not documented: nobody publishes the rule. What I could not establish: whether a signup from any particular country succeeds, because that requires making an account and I did not; and the true minimum boot volume, because the page states 47 GB and 50 GB in two paragraphs.

old: SIGNUP PATH, read today. There is no Google Cloud signup page: cloud.google.com/signup returns a 404 and console.cloud.google.com/freetrial redirects to a Google account signup at accounts.cloud.google.com, whose first field is an email address. The Cloud form comes after the Google account exists and asks for name, address and payment method, and in some countries a bank account instead. A card is not optional: 'you must provide a credit card or other payment method'. THE HOLD IS 0.00 TO 1.00 USD, published on the free-features page, and it is the widest published range of the three providers: a bank may convert it and hold it for 'a few days to a month'. THE DEBIT RULE has a second half that matters more than the first: debit is accepted with a Visa or Mastercard logo, but 'Debit cards that require two-factor authentication aren't accepted for payment', which excludes most European and many Asian debit cards that push a one-time password by SMS. Prepaid and virtual are refused. THE GRANT IS TWO PRODUCTS. The always-free e2-micro is a permanent monthly allowance. The USD 300 is a 90-day trial on the same billing account, and when it closes Google stops 'all of its associated projects and resources' - the documentation does not carve out the always-free instance the way Oracle's FAQ does for Always Free. A user who wants the e2-micro to survive month four has to upgrade to a paid billing account, and then the always-free allowance still covers the instance and the bill is zero, but the account is now billable and the 1 GB egress overage is chargeable. That is the caveat, and it is the difference between this row and Oracle's. WHAT IT IS USABLE FOR: 1 GB a month of egress out of North America is 0.09 per cent of one TiB (1e9 bytes against 1.0995e12), so it is a relay, a scheduler, a monitoring node or an SSH jump box, and not a host. Inbound listen works and it has a public ephemeral IP, not a static one; a static IP is billed separately. The shape is 0.25 sustained vCPU with a 30-second burst, so anything CPU-bound is slow. What I could not establish: whether a phone number is required at signup, because no page read names one and the console form is behind a Google login I did not pass; the phrase 'Google accounts with only a phone number are not supported' is about the account type, not about a verification step.

The 20.0% is a ceiling, not a floor. The 12 payload successes sat on 7 distinct addresses, 6 of them ports on 45.74.31.42 alone, so the working pool is one relay with several doors. Nine of the 12 exited from an address other than the one listed (45.74.31.42's exits were GoDaddy, Contabo and Google addresses), so the address a caller picks is not the address the target sees, and with no metadata on any line there is nothing else to pick by.

Candidates for the 80% failure, each with what would refute it. (1) A stale, unpruned list: predicts a spread of timeouts and refusals, and 35 timeouts, 3 refusals, 3 EOF and 1 reset were observed, so it stands. (2) Padded or duplicated lines: predicts repeats, and all 8,047 entries are unique, so it is refuted for exact duplication and only weakened for scraping from other lists. (3) Live SOCKS5 servers demanding authentication, or something other than SOCKS5 on the port: predicts a reply to the version/method greeting followed by a rejection, and 4 lines answered no acceptable method while 1 served a Synology DiskStation login page instead of the target body, so it stands for a minority. (4) The probe host's own egress being filtered on odd ports: predicts failure clustered by port, and the 12 successes ran from the same machine in the same pass, which weakens it but does not exclude a per-port block. A 60-line single-day draw cannot separate (1) from (4); 500 lines twice in one day could.

The comparison handed to this record does not hold as written. The list is described as the worst of the metadata-free lists, but .tmp/lane4/results-speedx.json and results-speedx-t2.json measured 8.0% payload on 100 lines in each of two runs, against 20.0% here on 60, so openproxylist is second-lowest of the five lists measured in .tmp/lane4, not lowest. The ranking is weaker evidence than it looks for a second reason: 5,087 of the 8,047 openproxylist lines are byte-identical host:port pairs with TheSpeedX's socks5 list and all 1,730 of its addresses appear here, so the two lists share 63.2% of this list's lines and are not independent draws of capacity. Adding lists of this kind adds lines, not exits. No other dossier record is corrected by this finding, because no other ip-proxy record exists yet; the contradiction is with the wave brief and with those two probe files.

The vendor's claim is not what the probe found: the FAQ states All proxies are tested before being listed, while 12 of 60 carried a payload on the day they were listed. That sentence is quoted as the vendor's position and is not treated as a fact about the pool.

The live file served 7,877 lines the same day, which is consistent with the stated 10-minute rebuild and means the count is not stable enough to quote without a date.

One sample, one day: the yield rests on a single 60-line draw taken on 2026-10-24. What would settle it is 500 lines sampled twice on the same day, plus a re-check of these same 12 lines 24 hours later to measure how long a working line survives.

old: Three candidates for the 8 percent payload rate, tested rather than assumed. (1) The probe harness was at fault. Refuted for the payload measure: 8 of the same 100 lines carried a payload under the identical harness, and the failures split across five distinct error classes rather than one systematic failure, which is what per-host failure looks like and not what a broken client looks like. (2) The lines are stale, and the file is a large pool of long-dead addresses. Supported and not fully settled: 58 of 100 timed out and 19 failed at the socket, and the second run produced 15 handshakes against 17, so the population churns under the probe; but nothing here shows the file is unmaintained, only that most of its lines do not answer. (3) A vantage-point or diurnal effect on this machine. Not refuted, because two runs 23 minutes apart cannot separate it from a dead list, and only runs spread across a day could. The verdict rests on (2) with (3) open, and (3) does not change it: the payload rate would have to rise by an order of magnitude before the list became usable at the request volume. Weight: each rate is one sample of 100 lines drawn stratified across the three protocol files, taken twice, which is enough to show the yield is low and repeats and not enough to put an interval on it. A discrepancy between the assigned facts and the artefacts, recorded rather than smoothed. The facts give the working exits as OVH AS16276 twice, Contabo AS51167, DigitalOcean AS14061, Microsoft AS8075, GoDaddy AS26496 and AS398101, and Biznet AS17451. Re-deriving from the two named result files yields eight payload exits: OVH AS16276 twice, Biznet AS17451, Contabo AS51167, Microsoft AS8075 and GoDaddy AS26496, plus SCTS AS51004 and Liteserver AS60404, which are absent from the assigned list; DigitalOcean AS14061 and GoDaddy AS398101 appear in .tmp/lane4/exit-asn.json against addresses that are not payload exits in either named file, so they belong to the wider lane-4 set rather than to this provider's eight. The datacenter conclusion survives the correction, since seven of the eight resolved to hosting ASNs and the eighth, SCTS, is a cable ISP; what changes is the roster, not the finding, and the verdict does not rest on it. On shape: the assignment names the interface tokens api, cli, rest, socks5, http-proxy, wireguard, openvpn, web-ui and none, but scripts/dossier/schema.json closes interface[] to its own enum, which has no proxy-protocol token, and scripts/dossier/validate.py enforces that enum; an in-memory test of socks5 and http-proxy against the schema returned two enum errors, so writing them would turn the gate red for the whole dossier tree. The array therefore carries rest, matching dossier/ip-proxy/proxyscrape-free-list.json, and the three protocols are stated in interface_detail. That gap is a defect worth naming: an ip-proxy topic cannot express what it is about until the enum gains socks5, http-proxy and a static-file token. Searched dossier/ and docs/ for an existing record naming TheSpeedX or PROXY-List to correct; the only hit is dossier/ip-proxy/proxyscrape-free-list.json and it is a substring match on free-proxy-list rather than a mention of this provider, so this record corrects nothing outside itself.

old: SIGNUP PATH, read today. The account is created at https://linuxone.cloud.marist.edu/#/register?flag=VM, reached from IBM's front door at community.ibm.com/zsystems/l1cc/ by the 'Try Virtual Machines' link. The form is an Angular template, so I read it as raw HTML rather than as rendered text: email, password and confirmation, first name, last name, organization, country (a 242-option list defaulting to United States, with Viet Nam present), a project description of 75 to 500 characters, an optional event code, a Terms checkbox and reCAPTCHA v3. THE PHONE STEP IS GONE. The form in circulation, including IBM's own archived deployment guide, says 'Provide a mobile phone number that is capable of receiving SMS messages', and the live page still carries that block in its source - but it is inside HTML comments, the controller's submit payload has no phone field, and the SMS-code function is commented out. So the phone claim is superseded, and the row is email-only, which is why identity_cost.kind is 'email' rather than 'any-phone'. NO CARD, NO ADDRESS. address1 through zip are posted as empty strings by the controller. Organization is on the form but has no required attribute. WHAT STOPS A SIGNUP: manual review, not a gate. The form's own success message says the request 'may take up to one (1) business day to process' and that credentials arrive by email once approved, and it also has a refusal path, 'We need additional information to proceed with your registration.' IBM's front door additionally states that outlook.com and hotmail.com addresses are currently refused by the registration system, which is a documented, first-party, signup-level failure and the cheapest one to avoid. WHAT IT GRANTS: one virtual server, s390x, full sudo, a public IP, SSH-key-only access, 120 days. THE SHAPE IS STILL UNPUBLISHED. IBM names the flavors LinuxONE-Small and LinuxONE-Medium and never states their vCPU, memory or disk; the 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB figure is third-party and stays marked as such in extras.shape_source. The console fetches flavor values at runtime and I did not create an account to read them. NETWORK: the instance gets a public IP and a firewall that opens only SSH, so inbound listening works but every port has to be opened with iptables first; that is documented in IBM's deployment guide. EGRESS IS UNPUBLISHED, and I am not going to invent a figure; the terms instead reserve the right to throttle or terminate for 'excessive network, computing or other resources'. VERDICT CHANGED to trial-only from qualifies-with-caveat. The grant is a fixed 120-day term after which 'all resources will be cleared of your data', which is a trial with a hard stop and not a renewable free tier; the earlier verdict was written when the 120-day term was read as a re-registration cycle, and no page says a re-registration succeeds. An extension mechanism exists in the portal (a service/extend endpoint behind an emailed token) but nothing states that a virtual-server entitlement is eligible for it. old:
This record corrects dossier/egress/anchoredip.json, whose evidence entry reads 'space registered at RIPE NCC and announced from AS41800' with no registration class. That sentence invites the reading that AnchoredIP is an ISP holding a broadband allocation. RIPE RDAP read on 2026-10-24 returns 194.0.109.0/24 as KZ-TROPYNIN-NET-109, country KZ, type ASSIGNED PA, registrant lir-kz-individual-1-MNT and Tropynin Oleg, and the autnum object names AS41800 as TROPYNIN-AS under the same registrant. That is a personal provider-independent assignment in Kazakhstan, not an eyeball network, and the announced footprint is five IPv4 /24s plus one IPv6 /29, so every tenant sits inside 1,280 addresses. The vendor's own footer says the same thing: 'AnchoredIP - AS41800 - Karaganda, Kazakhstan'. The egress record must stop implying ISP registration; this record carries the measured class.

Three candidates were considered for what the space is, and each was tested. (1) An ISP with a broadband allocation: refuted, because the RDAP type is ASSIGNED PA and the registrant is an individual maintenance object rather than a LIR member. (2) A hosting provider's block re-announced by AnchoredIP: refuted, because the AS registrant and the address registrant are the same person. (3) A resold block from a larger carrier: not refuted and not confirmed, because the parent 194.0.108.0-194.0.111.255 was not walked up to the LIR that allocated it. That walk is what would settle it, and it was not run.

Two deviations from the brief are deliberate and both come from evidence read this session. First, identity_cost.kind is email and not anonymous. No card and no account is right, but POST /api/leases/ requires billing_email and the API page states 'A trial is one per billing email', so the email is the key the free offer is counted against; a reader planning several trials is misled by anonymous and not by email. Second, the registrant handle the brief gives as lrp-kz-individual-1-MNT reads lir-kz-individual-1-MNT in the live RDAP response; the record carries the measured string.

Interface is recorded as rest and cli because the enum in scripts/dossier/schema.json has no token for wireguard, web-ui, api, socks5 or http-proxy, so the WireGuard path, the dashboard and the MCP endpoint are carried in interface_detail rather than dropped or forced into a token that would be wrong. The egress quote is on /vs/fixie and not on /pricing, which is a second and smaller correction to the egress record, whose source_url for that sentence points at the pricing page.

What could not be settled: which /24 a leased address actually lands in. The vendor says the trial is 'a real address out of the same /24 our paying customers are in', and its own API example shows 194.0.108.99 while the RDAP sample is 194.0.109.0/24, so more than one /24 is in use and only a live lease would fix which. The latency figures are the vendor's measurements, not ours. And this rests on one sample: one /24 was classified out of the five announced, so the other four are unverified and the class claim is a claim about 194.0.109.0/24 rather than about the whole service.

old:
This record corrects dossier/egress/anchoredip.json, whose evidence entry reads 'space registered at RIPE NCC and announced from AS41800' with no registration class. That sentence invites the reading that AnchoredIP is an ISP holding a broadband allocation. RIPE RDAP read on 2026-10-24 returns 194.0.109.0/24 with country KZ, type ASSIGNED PA and registrant lir-kz-individual-1-MNT, an individual, and the autnum object for AS41800 sits under the same registrant. That is a personal provider-independent assignment in Kazakhstan, not an eyeball network, and the announced footprint is five IPv4 /24s plus one IPv6 /29, so every tenant sits inside 1,280 addresses. The vendor's own footer says the same thing: 'AnchoredIP - AS41800 - Karaganda, Kazakhstan'. The egress record must stop implying ISP registration; this record carries the measured class.

Each of three possible kinds of holder was tested for this space. (1) An ISP with a broadband allocation: refuted, because the RDAP type is ASSIGNED PA and the registrant is an individual maintenance object rather than a LIR member. (2) A hosting provider's block re-announced by AnchoredIP: refuted, because the AS registrant and the address registrant are the same person. (3) A resold block from a larger carrier: not refuted and not confirmed, because the parent 194.0.108.0-194.0.111.255 was not walked up to the LIR that allocated it. That walk is what would settle it, and it was not run.

Two deviations are deliberate and both come from the evidence. First, identity_cost.kind is email and not anonymous. No card and no account is right, but POST /api/leases/ requires billing_email and the API page states 'A trial is one per billing email', so the email is the key the free offer is counted against; a reader planning several trials is misled by anonymous and not by email. Second, the registrant handle reads lir-kz-individual-1-MNT in the live RDAP response; the record carries the measured string.

Interface is recorded as rest and cli because the enum in scripts/dossier/schema.json has no token for wireguard, web-ui, api, socks5 or http-proxy, so the WireGuard path, the dashboard and the MCP endpoint are carried in interface_detail rather than dropped or forced into a token that would be wrong. The egress quote is on /vs/fixie and not on /pricing, which the egress record's source_url for that sentence points at.

What could not be settled: which /24 a leased address actually lands in. The vendor says the trial is 'a real address out of the same /24 our paying customers are in', and its own API example shows 194.0.108.99 while the RDAP sample is 194.0.109.0/24, so more than one /24 is in use and only a live lease would fix which. The latency figures are the vendor's measurements, not ours. And this rests on one sample: one /24 was classified out of the five announced, so the other four are unverified and the class claim is a claim about 194.0.109.0/24 rather than about the whole service.
